There is now clear evidence that a number of crucial system-level tipping points have been reached, in some cases decades to centuries earlier than had been projected. Seven of nine sustainable planetary boundaries have already been exceeded.

A tipping point is a threshold beyond which large change is initiated in a system and becomes self-perpetuating, and the change is often abrupt and irreversible on long timescales.42 Passing these thresholds may constitute an ecological point of no return, after which it may be practically impossible to return the climate to pre-industrial (Holocene) stability. Tipping points may interact to form tipping cascades that act to further accelerate the rate of warming and climate impacts (see Section 7).
